headline: Google ADK 2.14 graduates 42 components to stable and closes prompt-injection hole
summary: Google's Agent Development Kit 2.14.0 moves 42 components to stable, signifying a shift towards production readiness for agent frameworks. It also quietly patches a critical prompt-injection vulnerability.
details: Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) 2.14.0, released November 7, marks a significant step for multi-agent systems. The update graduates 42 components, including 26 modules and 16 toolset integrations, from experimental to stable status. This signals a move from experimental development to production-ready applications.

A key security enhancement in ADK 2.14.0 addresses a prompt-injection vulnerability. The RunSkillScriptTool no longer accepts free-form shell commands, requiring structured arguments and scripts from a validated directory. This prevents malicious model outputs from executing arbitrary shell commands.

The release also introduces a new TeamsRunner, embedding ADK agents directly into Microsoft Teams. This integration aims to make agents more accessible and useful within existing work conversations, rather than requiring separate consoles.

Evaluation capabilities are enhanced with MultiRunConfig, allowing concurrent, multiple runs for each evaluation case. This improves the reliability of agent evaluations by combining scores and pass rates across runs, acknowledging the inherent nondeterminism of single-run evaluations.

Tool argument validation is upgraded with ToolArgsMatcher, featuring four modes including LLM-backed semantic matching. This advanced checking ensures arguments carry the correct intent, even with varied phrasing, reducing false negatives in evaluations.

Other additions include MongoDbMemoryService with vector-search and TTL expiry for agent memory, an adk generate_agent_card CLI command, and an OpenAI Decisions integration. Google claims a 23% speed increase and 9% lower peak memory for a 30-node workflow, though benchmarks lack specific baselines.

headline_marked: [[Open-weight AI models sweep Wordle]] but struggle with Mastermind in new tournament
headline: Open-weight AI models sweep Wordle but struggle with Mastermind in new tournament
summary: Six open-weight AI models were tested in a seeded tournament, with most excelling at Wordle but showing varied performance in Mastermind, highlighting challenges in letter manipulation and pure deduction.
details: A new tournament pitted six open-weight AI models against Wordle and Mastermind, revealing distinct strengths and weaknesses. The study, conducted by an AI agent from Zero Human Company, aimed to rigorously measure AI capabilities in game-based scenarios. Results showed a clear split: models generally dominated Wordle, but Mastermind sharply differentiated their deductive skills.

The choice of Wordle and Mastermind was deliberate, targeting known challenges for language models. Wordle tests the manipulation of individual letters, a task often complicated by tokenization in LLMs. Mastermind, devoid of language, reduces the challenge to pure deduction under strict rules.

The Wordle variant, dubbed WORDGATE, used 5-letter words with 6 guesses and standard feedback, including duplicate letter rules. Answer words came from a published list of 1,329 candidates, and valid guesses from a 15,921-word list. Four consecutive invalid replies resulted in a loss.

Mastermind followed classic rules: 4 pegs, 6 colors (A–F), with duplicates allowed, totaling 1,296 possible codes. Models had 8 guesses, receiving feedback on exact and partial matches after each attempt. Both games were self-hosted HTTP services, with each guess triggering a fresh, stateless LLM call.

For Wordle, six of the seven tested cells won every game, often in a median of 4 guesses. One model, glm-5.3-flash, even won 5/5 games reading rendered boards as images, though it misparsed images more frequently (23% invalid turns vs. 15% on text). This suggests vision input was not a significant handicap.

Mastermind proved more challenging, with only three models successfully deducing every code within the 8-guess limit. gpt-oss:120b delivered a perfect performance, winning all five games in exactly 4 guesses with zero invalid replies. This highlights its strong deductive reasoning.

Conversely, one model, gemma4:31b, failed to win a single game, struggling with the game's format itself. This stark contrast underscores the varying levels of core deductive and letter-manipulation capabilities across different open-weight AI models.
